title: What are think tanks all about?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant (with Jerry sitting in) explain what think tanks are: nonprofit groups that research public problems and push evidence-based policy ideas toward the public and policymakers. They trace the history from Plato's Academy, through the Royal United Services Institution (1831), the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (1910), and the Brookings Institution (1916), to the post-World War Two proliferation and the RAND Corporation's technology work. They cover tax-exempt status and the 1950s congressional rules against partisanship, the rise of advocacy think tanks (Heritage Foundation, Center for American Progress, ALEC and the State Policy Network), donor influence and corporate funding (including the Koch-funded groups on climate science and the Brookings–Lennar San Francisco episode), the claim that think tanks are losing relevance to social media and the "death of expertise," and a listener mail segment about ballpoint pens.

segments.title: Opening banter and what a think tank is
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the name, then describe think tanks as nonprofit groups that research problems and push evidence-based policy ideas to the public and policymakers, noting the ideal of being nonpartisan and fact based.

segments.title: Early history: Plato's Academy and early modern think tanks
segments.summary: Plato's Academy is described as possibly the first think tank. The hosts then cite the Royal United Services Institution (1831), the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (1910), and the Brookings Institution (founded 1916 by Robert Brookings).

segments.title: Brookings, the New Deal, and the Marshall Plan
segments.summary: Brookings' influence after the Depression and its role in the New Deal and Marshall Plan are discussed, along with the claim that Brookings is labeled liberal but scores near the center on a liberal-leaning rating.

segments.title: RAND Corporation and technology research
segments.summary: RAND, whose name comes from research and development, is described as a think tank credited with ideas that led to computers, the Internet, spy satellites and the space program. Specialized versus broad think tanks are compared.

segments.title: Post-war proliferation, tax-exempt status, and rules against partisanship
segments.summary: After World War Two think tanks proliferated. Early philanthropists endowed them as government research arms. Tax-exempt status was granted, and in the 1950s Congress required them to avoid partisanship and candidate endorsements.

segments.title: Advocacy think tanks: Heritage, Center for American Progress, ALEC
segments.summary: Advocacy think tanks emerged that openly take sides. The Center for American Progress was founded after the 2000 Democratic loss; the Heritage Foundation's Reagan-era recommendations are described; ALEC and the State Policy Network are discussed as model-bill and litigation groups.

segments.title: Donors, corporate money, and loss of independence
segments.summary: The hosts explain that funding has shifted from unrestricted philanthropy to directed, results-oriented donations and corporate money. Billionaire-funded climate science skepticism through Atlas Economic Research Foundation and International Policy Network is cited. A Chinatown reference illustrates the theme, and the hosts argue donors affect research on both sides.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: A short ad break between segments.

segments.title: Walton Family Foundation, Brookings corporate deals, and the death of expertise
segments.summary: The Walton Family Foundation's funding of think tanks is discussed, along with Brookings' corporate solicitations and the Lennar San Francisco project, described as lobbying. The hosts discuss donor previews, self-censorship, the 'death of expertise,' and the claim that social media and Ted talks have outpaced think tanks, including the RAND vaccine-autism research.

segments.title: Listener mail: ballpoint pen addiction
segments.summary: A listener writes about their fondness for gel rollerball pens and the Pilot V Ball pen, and thermal paper for restaurant checks. The hosts respond to pen recommendations.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts suggest further reading and invite listeners to contact the show via social media or email.
